subtopic_detail: Erythrocytosis detected on routine monitoring during masculinising hormone therapy
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared care for a 27 year old trans man who has been receiving intramuscular testosterone undecanoate 1000 mg every 12 weeks for 14 months. He feels well, works night shifts as a baker, and has no chest pain, breathlessness or visual symptoms.

He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and has done so since he was 18. He takes no other regular medicines and drinks alcohol rarely. His last injection was six weeks ago and he attends today for his routine monitoring bloods, which you review with him in the room.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.57 (0.40-0.54), haemoglobin 188 g/L (130-175), ferritin within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, total testosterone 17 nmol/L (8-27)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of these results?

options.text: Continue the current dose and interval, and repeat the full blood count in 12 months
options.rationale: A haematocrit above the upper reference limit is the commonest dose related adverse effect of testosterone and waiting a year allows it to climb further. Annual review would be appropriate only if the haematocrit were within range. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Cease testosterone permanently and refer him back to the gender service for further review
options.rationale: Abrupt permanent cessation is disproportionate to a dose related and reversible effect, and it exposes him to the distress and vasomotor symptoms of hormone withdrawal. Dose reduction achieves the same haematological goal without stopping affirming care. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Reduce the testosterone dose, offer smoking cessation support, and repeat in three months
options.rationale: Testosterone driven erythrocytosis is dose dependent, and smoking is an additive stimulus to red cell mass, so the two modifiable drivers are addressed together and the response is checked at the next injection cycle. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy; Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Commence low dose aspirin and continue testosterone at the current dose and interval
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy does not lower red cell mass and is not indicated for primary prevention at his age, so the underlying driver would continue unchecked. It would be reasonable only if he had an established arterial indication. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer him for venesection today and continue testosterone at the current dose and interval
options.rationale: Venesection treats the number without removing the stimulus, so the haematocrit rebounds and iron stores fall with repeated procedures. It is reserved for a haematocrit that stays high despite dose reduction or for symptomatic hyperviscosity. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

explanation.summary: Masculinising hormone therapy requires structured monitoring of haematocrit, blood pressure, lipids and liver function, most intensively in the first year and then at least annually. Erythrocytosis is the commonest dose related adverse effect and is more likely with intramuscular depot preparations, which produce higher peak concentrations than transdermal gel. Smoking, obstructive sleep apnoea and chronic hypoxia are additive stimuli and should be sought whenever the haematocrit rises. In context, a gender affirming prescription is managed like any other long term therapy: the monitoring result changes the dose rather than the goal of care.
key_points: Haematocrit above the upper reference limit on testosterone prompts dose reduction and a search for additive drivers rather than cessation of therapy.
Intramuscular depot testosterone produces higher peaks and more erythrocytosis than transdermal preparations, so a formulation change is an alternative to dose reduction.
Smoking and untreated obstructive sleep apnoea both raise red cell mass and are modifiable at the same visit.
Venesection is a salvage measure for persistent or symptomatic erythrocytosis, not a first response.
explanation.pearls: Trough testosterone is measured immediately before the next intramuscular dose; a level taken mid cycle looks reassuring even when peak driven erythrocytosis is occurring.

sources.label: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy
Australian Medicines Handbook

subtopic_detail: Choosing an oestrogen formulation when vascular risk factors are present
stem:
A 32 year old trans woman attends your general practice asking to move her hormone therapy into supervised care. For the past seven months she has been taking oestrogen tablets bought through an overseas website, without any monitoring.

She smokes 10 cigarettes a day. She has had migraine with visual aura roughly monthly since her twenties, and her mother had a pulmonary embolism at 52. Her body mass index is 31 kg/m2. She has no personal history of venous thromboembolism. She wants to continue feminising therapy and asks what you would put her on.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, fasting lipids within normal limits, oestradiol 210 pmol/L, prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: Which regimen would you first recommend?

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol patch 50 micrograms per 24 hours, with dose review in three months
options.rationale: Transdermal oestradiol avoids first pass hepatic induction of clotting factors and carries the lowest thrombotic risk, which is the deciding consideration given smoking, migraine with aura and raised body mass index. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy; Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Oral ethinyloestradiol 30 micrograms daily, with a dose review in three months
options.rationale: Ethinyloestradiol has the highest thrombotic risk of the available oestrogens and is specifically avoided in gender affirming regimens for that reason. It is the agent most likely to be found in unregulated online products. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Oral conjugated equine oestrogens 1.25 mg daily, with dose review in three months
options.rationale: Conjugated equine oestrogens cannot be monitored with serum oestradiol levels and carry greater thrombotic risk than transdermal oestradiol. They are not a recommended option for feminising therapy in Australia. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Intramuscular oestradiol valerate 20 mg once every two weeks, with dose review in three months
options.rationale: Injectable oestradiol produces wide peaks and troughs and is generally reserved for people who cannot tolerate or absorb other routes. It is a second line choice rather than the opening regimen for someone with vascular risk factors. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Withhold all oestrogen until she stops smoking, with readiness review in three months
options.rationale: Making affirming care conditional on smoking cessation drives people back to unmonitored overseas supply, which is the greater risk here. Cessation is offered alongside treatment rather than as a gate to it. (Source: RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria)
source_refs: RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria

explanation.summary: Feminising hormone therapy in Australia uses 17 beta oestradiol, given orally, transdermally or by injection, with an antiandrogen where testes are present. Route selection is driven mainly by thrombotic risk: the first pass hepatic effect of oral oestrogen raises procoagulant factors, and ethinyloestradiol does so most strongly. Serum oestradiol can be monitored on oestradiol preparations, which supports dose titration and detects supratherapeutic self dosing. In context, people who have been self medicating are at their most vulnerable at the point of transfer into supervised care, and a regimen they can stay on matters more than the theoretically ideal one they abandon.
key_points: Transdermal oestradiol is preferred where there is smoking, obesity, migraine with aura, age over 45 or a thrombophilia risk.
Ethinyloestradiol is avoided in gender affirming regimens because of its disproportionate thrombotic risk.
Serum oestradiol monitoring is possible on oestradiol but not on conjugated equine oestrogens.
Refusing to prescribe until a risk factor is modified predictably returns the person to unmonitored online supply.
explanation.pearls: Migraine with aura is a contraindication to ethinyloestradiol containing preparations but not to transdermal oestradiol, which is why the route rather than the hormone is the decision point.

subtopic_detail: New vaginal bleeding after established amenorrhoea on testosterone
stem:
A 34 year old trans man comes to your clinic because he has been getting light bleeding on and off for six weeks, which he describes as spotting that stains his underwear. He has been on testosterone gel for three years and had no bleeding at all for the 30 months before this.

He has never had a cervical screening test and finds pelvic examination intolerable. He has not had chest or genital surgery and takes no other medicines. He has no pelvic pain, and his last testosterone level and haematocrit were within the expected range.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, no palpable mass, external examination declined
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 141 g/L (130-175), total testosterone 19 nmol/L (8-27), urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the testosterone dose and review the bleeding pattern again in three months
options.rationale: His testosterone level is already in the target range, so raising the dose adds erythrocytosis risk without investigating the bleeding. Dose adjustment is reasonable only for breakthrough bleeding with a subtherapeutic level. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Prescribe a course of norethisterone and review the bleeding pattern again in three months
options.rationale: Progestogen suppresses the bleeding and therefore masks the finding that needs explaining, which is new bleeding after prolonged amenorrhoea. It has a role once structural and neoplastic causes have been excluded. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Reassure him this is an expected effect of testosterone and review again in three months
options.rationale: Bleeding that returns after 30 months of amenorrhoea is not an expected effect and attributing it to hormones is the classic overshadowing error in trans health. Early breakthrough bleeding in the first months of therapy is a different situation. (Source: RACGP: Trans and gender diverse health care in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Trans and gender diverse health care in general practice

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound and offer a self collected cervical screening test now
options.rationale: New bleeding after established amenorrhoea requires assessment of the endometrium and cervix, and self collection removes the barrier of speculum examination while giving an equally valid primary human papillomavirus result. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: National Cervical Screening Guidelines)
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: National Cervical Screening Guidelines

options.text: Refer him for endometrial ablation and review the bleeding pattern again in three months
options.rationale: Ablation is a treatment for established benign heavy bleeding and would destroy the tissue needed for diagnosis. Proceeding to it without imaging or screening skips the entire assessment step. (Source: RACGP: Trans and gender diverse health care in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Trans and gender diverse health care in general practice

explanation.summary: Organ based screening and assessment apply regardless of a person's gender: anyone with a cervix who has ever been sexually active remains eligible for cervical screening, and anyone with an endometrium can develop endometrial pathology. Testosterone causes atrophic change in the vaginal and cervical epithelium, which makes speculum examination painful and raises the rate of unsatisfactory conventional samples. Self collected vaginal samples for primary human papillomavirus testing are available to all eligible screening participants in Australia and remove that barrier. In context, under-screening in trans and gender diverse people is driven less by refusal than by pathways that assume the examination will happen the usual way.
key_points: Bleeding that resumes after prolonged testosterone induced amenorrhoea is investigated, not attributed to the hormone.
Self collected primary human papillomavirus testing is a valid screening option and removes the speculum barrier.
Testosterone induced atrophy increases unsatisfactory conventional cytology rates, so topical oestrogen may be needed before any clinician collected sample.
Screening is decided by the organs a person has, not by the gender recorded in the file.
explanation.pearls: A person on testosterone who still has a uterus can ovulate and conceive, so a negative pregnancy test belongs in the workup of new bleeding even after years of amenorrhoea.

Australian Medicines Handbook

subtopic_detail: Antiandrogen adverse effects during feminising therapy
stem:
A 28 year old trans woman has been on oestradiol valerate 6 mg daily and cyproterone acetate 100 mg daily for 10 months, prescribed before she moved interstate and never reviewed since.

Over the past three months she has felt flat and persistently tired, and she has noticed a milky discharge from both nipples when she showers. She has no headaches and no change in her vision. She is not taking an antipsychotic or any other regular medicine. She is pleased with her physical changes and does not want feminising therapy interrupted.

data_table.Examination: Visual fields full to confrontation, fundoscopy normal, bilateral expressible milky nipple discharge, no breast mass
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1450 mIU/L (less than 600), alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 35), oestradiol 380 pmol/L, total testosterone less than 0.5 nmol/L, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Continue the current regimen unchanged and repeat the prolactin level in six months
options.rationale: Both the prolactin rise and the transaminase rise are dose related effects of high dose cyproterone and will persist or worsen if nothing changes. Six monthly monitoring is appropriate only once the offending dose has been addressed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease cyproterone, start spironolactone 100 mg daily, and repeat levels in eight weeks
options.rationale: Hyperprolactinaemia and hepatotoxicity from cyproterone are dose dependent and reverse on withdrawal, and spironolactone maintains androgen blockade without either effect. Repeating the levels at eight weeks confirms the drug was the cause. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Start cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly and continue the current antiandrogen dose
options.rationale: A dopamine agonist treats the laboratory abnormality while leaving the causative drug in place, and it does nothing for the liver derangement. Cabergoline is for a prolactinoma, not for drug induced hyperprolactinaemia with a removable cause. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease oestradiol, continue cyproterone, and repeat the prolactin level in eight weeks
options.rationale: This stops the medicine that is delivering her feminising effects and retains the one responsible for the adverse effects, since cyproterone rather than oestradiol is the dominant driver of prolactin at this dose. The relationship between the two agents is the point of discrimination here. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary before making any change to therapy
options.rationale: Imaging first is indicated when there is no drug explanation, visual field loss, or a prolactin that stays high after the suspect drug is withdrawn. Here a sufficient pharmacological cause is present and imaging can follow if the level does not settle. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Cyproterone acetate is an effective antiandrogen but its adverse effects, including hyperprolactinaemia, hepatotoxicity, mood disturbance and meningioma, are dose and duration dependent. Australian practice has moved to much lower doses, typically 12.5 to 25 mg daily or less, or to spironolactone, because androgen suppression is achieved at doses far below those used historically. Spironolactone requires potassium and renal monitoring but does not raise prolactin. In context, a person who arrives on an inherited high dose regimen needs the regimen reviewed rather than the symptoms treated one at a time.
key_points: Cyproterone adverse effects are dose dependent, so dose reduction or a switch resolves most of them.
Drug induced hyperprolactinaemia with a clear pharmacological cause and no neurological signs does not need imaging first.
Spironolactone is the alternative antiandrogen and needs potassium and renal function monitoring instead.
Low mood during feminising therapy has drug related causes that should be excluded before it is treated as a primary mood disorder.
explanation.pearls: Cyproterone doses above 25 mg daily give no additional androgen suppression in feminising therapy but carry most of the meningioma and hepatotoxicity risk, which is why the modern Australian starting dose is 12.5 mg.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook
AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

subtopic_detail: Pregnancy prevention while established on masculinising hormone therapy
stem:
A 22 year old trans man attends for a sexual health check. He has been on testosterone for 10 months and has had no periods for the last seven of those.

He has a new male partner and they have been having condomless vaginal sex for about two months. He has a uterus and ovaries and has had no surgery. He tells you he assumed that being on testosterone meant he could not get pregnant. He does not want to be pregnant now or in the next few years, but is unsure about the longer term.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, abdominal examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative, sexually transmitted infection screen pending, haemoglobin and haematocrit within normal limits

lead_in: What would you first recommend for pregnancy prevention?

options.text: Advise that no contraception is required while amenorrhoea continues on testosterone
options.rationale: Testosterone suppresses menstruation but does not reliably suppress ovulation, and pregnancies occur in people who are amenorrhoeic on it. Amenorrhoea is therefore not evidence of contraceptive cover. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Prescribe a combined oral contraceptive containing ethinyloestradiol and levonorgestrel
options.rationale: An oestrogen containing method opposes the effects he is seeking and commonly causes distress, and it offers no advantage over progestogen only options. It would be considered only if a progestogen containing method were unsuitable. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Advise fertility awareness based methods with condoms while he remains amenorrhoeic
options.rationale: Fertility awareness depends on tracking a cycle he no longer has, so there is nothing to time abstinence against. Typical use failure rates are also far higher than any long acting method. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Increase the testosterone dose to maintain amenorrhoea and supply condoms alone
options.rationale: Raising the dose neither guarantees anovulation nor provides contraception, and it adds erythrocytosis risk. Condoms alone have a typical use failure rate around 13 percent per year. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Offer a levonorgestrel intrauterine device now and continue his current testosterone
options.rationale: A progestogen only long acting method gives the lowest failure rate, does not counteract masculinising effects, and supports ongoing amenorrhoea. Insertion under local or general anaesthetic can be arranged if examination is intolerable. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

explanation.summary: Testosterone is teratogenic and is not a contraceptive, yet the belief that it prevents pregnancy is common and is reinforced by the amenorrhoea it produces. Progestogen only methods, including the levonorgestrel intrauterine device, the etonogestrel implant and depot medroxyprogesterone, are all compatible with masculinising therapy and do not oppose its effects. Fertility preservation should be discussed before hormones are started and revisited periodically, because prolonged testosterone exposure has uncertain effects on ovarian reserve. In context, sexual and reproductive health needs do not disappear when a person transitions, and assuming they do is how unintended pregnancies and missed infections happen.
key_points: Testosterone induced amenorrhoea does not reliably prevent ovulation, so contraception is still required.
Progestogen only long acting methods are preferred because they do not oppose masculinising effects.
Oestrogen containing contraception is usually avoided for reasons of both effect and distress.
Fertility preservation counselling is revisited over time rather than being a single pre-treatment conversation.
explanation.pearls: Testosterone is category D in pregnancy and causes virilisation of a female fetus, so an unplanned pregnancy on testosterone is an urgent rather than routine review.

AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

subtopic_detail: Sequencing gender assessment alongside a first episode of psychosis
stem:
You are the registrar on an early psychosis team reviewing a 19 year old trans woman admitted three weeks ago with a four month history of persecutory beliefs about her neighbours and auditory hallucinations. She is responding to risperidone and her beliefs are no longer held with conviction.

She has been living as a woman since she was 16 and asks daily about starting hormone therapy. Her mother's collateral history describes her consistently identifying as female since the age of 12, with no change during this episode. The psychotic content has never involved her gender or her body. The team is divided about what to do with her request.

data_table.Examination: Calm and cooperative, no formal thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance in the past week, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits, urine drug screen negative on admission

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Continue antipsychotic treatment and refer concurrently to the gender service for assessment
options.rationale: A stable, long predating and non delusional gender identity is assessed on its own merits, and parallel referral avoids the indefinite deferral that drives disengagement and self medication. Treating the psychosis remains the immediate clinical priority. (Source: RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria)
source_refs: RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria

options.text: Defer gender service referral until she has been free of psychotic symptoms for two years
options.rationale: No Australian standard sets a fixed symptom free period before gender assessment, and a two year block is the kind of blanket gatekeeping that predicts disengagement and unmonitored online hormone use. A delay is justified only by an unresolved question about capacity. (Source: RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria)
source_refs: RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria

options.text: Refer to the gender service and withhold antipsychotic treatment until assessment is complete
options.rationale: Stopping effective treatment during a first episode risks relapse and prolongs the duration of untreated psychosis, which worsens functional outcome. The two decisions are not in competition. (Source: Orygen: Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis)
source_refs: Orygen: Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

options.text: Interpret her stated gender identity as part of the delusional system and treat accordingly
options.rationale: The identity predates the illness by seven years, never featured in the psychotic content, and has not shifted with treatment, which is the opposite of a delusional belief. This would be correct only if the identity had emerged within the episode and moved with symptom severity. (Source: RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria)
source_refs: RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria

options.text: Commence feminising hormone therapy today and review the psychotic symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Hormone initiation follows assessment of capacity, baseline investigations and a discussion of fertility, none of which has occurred during this admission. Starting today skips the process rather than accelerating access. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

explanation.summary: Gender diverse people develop the same psychiatric illnesses as anyone else, and a co-occurring illness neither explains nor invalidates gender identity. The clinical question is whether the identity is stable and independent of the illness course, which is answered with a developmental and collateral history rather than by waiting. Where gender themes do appear within psychotic content, they typically emerge with the episode, fluctuate with symptom severity, and resolve with treatment. In context, blanket deferral of gender assessment until a person is entirely well is a common cause of disengagement from mental health services and of unsupervised hormone use.
key_points: A gender identity that predates the illness, is stable over years and never appears in psychotic content is assessed independently of the illness.
Delusional gender related content emerges with the episode and moves with symptom severity.
Parallel referral avoids the disengagement and self medication that follow indefinite deferral.
Capacity, not diagnosis, determines whether a person can consent to hormone therapy.
explanation.pearls: Risperidone raises prolactin, which a person on feminising therapy may welcome but which still requires monitoring, and this interaction is a reason to involve the gender service early rather than late.

sources.label: RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria
Orygen: Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis
AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

subtopic_detail: Medical instability thresholds in a gender diverse young person with restrictive eating
stem:
A 17 year old non binary young person, who uses they and them pronouns, is brought to your clinic by a parent after losing 12 kg over five months. They have been eating one small meal a day and running before school.

They tell you that the eating changes began as a way to stop their periods and to flatten their chest, and that the weight loss has done both. They are on a waiting list for a gender service and are not on any hormone therapy. They deny wanting to harm themselves. They feel cold constantly and fainted once last week while getting out of bed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 41 beats per minute, blood pressure 86/54 mmHg lying with a fall of 22 mmHg systolic on standing, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 35.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 15.1 kg/m2, cool peripheries, dry skin, no oedema, alert and oriented
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), phosphate 0.75 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), magnesium within normal limits, electrocardiogram sinus bradycardia with corrected QT interval 468 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Refer to a community eating disorder service for outpatient family based treatment this week
options.rationale: Outpatient family based treatment is the right medium term plan but assumes medical stability, which the bradycardia, postural drop and hypothermia exclude. It becomes appropriate after refeeding has restored cardiovascular stability. (Source: NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit)

options.text: Refer to the gender service for prioritised assessment before starting eating disorder treatment
options.rationale: Addressing gender related distress is part of the longer term plan but cannot precede treatment of a life threatening physiological state. Sequencing it first would leave the immediate cardiac risk untreated. (Source: RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria)
source_refs: RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria

options.text: Arrange admission to hospital today for supervised refeeding and continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: A pulse under 50 beats per minute, a postural systolic fall over 20 mmHg, hypothermia and hypokalaemia each independently meet Australian criteria for inpatient medical stabilisation, and refeeding must be supervised because of the phosphate shift risk. (Source: NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit)

options.text: Commence olanzapine 2.5 mg at night and arrange outpatient dietitian review within the week
options.rationale: Olanzapine has a limited adjunctive role in weight restoration and none in acute medical stabilisation, and it prolongs the corrected QT interval that is already 468 ms. Pharmacotherapy does not substitute for refeeding. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Arrange twice weekly general practice weight and vital sign checks with supervised family meals
options.rationale: Monitoring in the community detects deterioration but does not treat it, and this young person has already deteriorated past the threshold at which it is safe. That plan suits a medically stable presentation with an intact home support structure. (Source: NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit)

explanation.summary: Restrictive eating disorders are over-represented in trans and gender diverse young people, and restriction is sometimes used to suppress secondary sex characteristics, which links the two problems but does not change the acute management. Australian admission criteria are physiological: bradycardia under 50 beats per minute, a postural systolic drop over 20 mmHg, hypothermia, electrolyte derangement and a prolonged corrected QT interval. Refeeding syndrome risk is highest in the first week and is monitored with daily phosphate, magnesium and potassium. In context, the gender related meaning of the restriction shapes the therapy that follows but never delays medical stabilisation.
key_points: Admission thresholds are physiological and are met by bradycardia, postural drop, hypothermia or electrolyte derangement regardless of body mass index.
A low-normal phosphate before refeeding predicts a fall once feeding starts, so daily electrolytes are mandatory in the first week.
Suppression of menstruation or chest development can be a motivation for restriction in gender diverse young people and should be asked about directly.
Gender affirming care and eating disorder treatment run in parallel once the person is medically stable.
explanation.pearls: A corrected QT interval over 460 ms in a person with an eating disorder makes any QT prolonging medicine, including olanzapine and ondansetron, a decision for the admitting team rather than a routine prescription.

sources.label: NSW Health Eating Disorders Toolkit
Australian Medicines Handbook
RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria

subtopic_detail: Raised potassium in a person taking spironolactone as an antiandrogen
stem:
A 36 year old trans woman attends for routine review. She has taken oestradiol valerate 6 mg daily and spironolactone 200 mg daily for 14 months and is happy with her progress.

Six weeks ago another doctor at the practice started her on perindopril for hypertension. She feels well, with no palpitations, weakness or muscle cramps. She takes no over the counter medicines and uses no salt substitutes. You review the monitoring bloods taken yesterday before she leaves.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 5.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 94 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL/min/1.73m2, electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with normal T wave morphology

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue both medicines at current doses and repeat the potassium level in three months
options.rationale: A potassium of 5.9 mmol/L is already in the range where arrhythmia risk rises and it will climb further while both potassium retaining drugs continue. Three monthly monitoring suits a level within the reference range. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease the oestradiol, continue spironolactone at the current dose, and repeat in one week
options.rationale: Oestradiol does not raise potassium, so stopping it removes her feminising therapy while leaving the responsible agent untouched. The distinction between the two medicines is the point being tested. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer her to the emergency department today for insulin dextrose and cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Emergency shifting therapy is for potassium above about 6.5 mmol/L or any level with electrocardiographic change, neither of which applies here. Her electrocardiogram is normal and the cause is removable in the community. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Electrolyte disorders)

options.text: Cease spironolactone permanently and offer her no alternative antiandrogen agent from now on
options.rationale: Withdrawing androgen blockade altogether allows testosterone effects to return and is not required, since low dose cyproterone or a gonadotropin releasing hormone analogue are alternatives. Permanent cessation without replacement is a disproportionate response. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Withhold spironolactone, review the perindopril, and repeat the potassium in one week
options.rationale: Two potassium retaining drugs were combined and the rise followed the second one, so both are addressed and the level is rechecked within a week before androgen blockade is re-established at a lower dose or with another agent. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Electrolyte disorders)

explanation.summary: Spironolactone is widely used as an antiandrogen in feminising therapy at doses of 100 to 200 mg daily, well above those used in cardiac failure, and hyperkalaemia is its dose limiting adverse effect. Risk multiplies when it is combined with an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor, an angiotensin receptor blocker, a non steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, trimethoprim or a potassium supplement. Potassium and renal function are checked before starting, at four to six weeks, and after any dose change or new interacting prescription. In context, people receiving gender affirming care are frequently prescribed for by several doctors, and the interaction risk sits in the gaps between them.
key_points: Spironolactone doses used for androgen blockade are far higher than cardiology doses, so hyperkalaemia risk is correspondingly higher.
Adding an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor, trimethoprim or a non steroidal anti-inflammatory drug is the usual precipitant.
Emergency potassium lowering is reserved for levels above about 6.5 mmol/L or any electrocardiographic change.
Androgen blockade is re-established with a lower dose or an alternative agent rather than abandoned.
explanation.pearls: Check potassium and creatinine four to six weeks after starting spironolactone and again after any new interacting prescription, because the person often feels entirely well at a level of 6 mmol/L.

subtopic_detail: Legal authorisation for stage two hormone treatment when parents disagree
stem:
You are the registrar at a multidisciplinary gender service reviewing a 16 year old trans boy who has been on puberty suppression for 18 months. The service has diagnosed gender dysphoria and the team, including the treating psychiatrist and paediatric endocrinologist, has assessed him as competent to consent to testosterone.

He lives with his mother, who supports the treatment and has signed the consent form. His father, who shares parental responsibility under a parenting order, has written to the service stating that he does not accept the diagnosis and opposes any hormone treatment. The young person is clear and consistent about wanting to proceed, and the clinic appointment today is to plan next steps.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage suppressed, height and weight tracking along the 50th centile, mood euthymic, no self harm
data_table.Investigations: Bone age consistent with chronological age, bone mineral density within expected range, liver function and lipids within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before testosterone can be commenced?

options.text: Proceed on his own consent, since the treating team has assessed him as competent to decide
options.rationale: Competence removes the need for court involvement only when the young person, both parents and the treating team all agree. A dispute by a person with parental responsibility about the diagnosis or the treatment reinstates the requirement for authorisation. (Source: Re Imogen (No 6) [2020] FamCA 761)

options.text: Apply to the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia for authorisation of the treatment
options.rationale: Where a parent or the treating doctor disputes the diagnosis, the young person's capacity, or the proposed treatment, an application must be made and the treatment cannot lawfully start until the court determines it. (Source: Re Imogen (No 6) [2020] FamCA 761)

options.text: Proceed with the consenting parent's authority, documenting the other parent's objection in full
options.rationale: Where parental responsibility is shared, the consent of one parent does not resolve a dispute about a major long term issue, and documenting the objection does not confer authority to treat. Careful documentation is necessary but is not the legal step required. (Source: Re Imogen (No 6) [2020] FamCA 761)

options.text: Refer the disagreement to the hospital clinical ethics committee for a binding determination
options.rationale: An ethics committee can advise the team but has no power to authorise treatment or to override a parental objection. Its advice is valuable in parallel with, not instead of, the application. (Source: Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents, Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne)
source_refs: Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents, Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne

options.text: Defer all hormone treatment until he turns eighteen and can give consent as an adult
options.rationale: Two years of additional suppression carries its own bone density and psychosocial costs, and deferral is not the remedy the law provides for a parental dispute. It would also make the decision by inaction rather than by determination. (Source: Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents, Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne)
source_refs: Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents, Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne

explanation.summary: Australian law on adolescent gender affirming treatment has moved in stages. Court authorisation was once required for all stage two hormone treatment, then Re Kelvin in 2017 removed that requirement where the young person is competent and there is no dispute, and Re Imogen in 2020 clarified that a dispute by a parent or the treating doctor about diagnosis, capacity or treatment returns the matter to the court. Puberty suppression can continue while an application is on foot, which is why the timing of the dispute matters clinically as well as legally. In context, the frequent error is to apply the Re Kelvin rule to a disputed case because the young person is plainly competent, when competence is only one of the three things that must be uncontested.
key_points: Re Kelvin removed the need for court authorisation only where the young person is competent and there is no dispute.
Re Imogen requires an application where a parent or the treating doctor disputes diagnosis, capacity or treatment.
Shared parental responsibility means one parent's consent does not settle a major long term issue.
A clinical ethics committee advises but cannot authorise treatment or override an objection.
explanation.pearls: Puberty suppression may lawfully continue while a Family Court application about stage two treatment is pending, which preserves the clinical position without pre-empting the determination.

Australian Standards of Care and Treatment Guidelines for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents, Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne

subtopic_detail: Perceptual experiences of a deceased relative during bereavement in a resettled family
stem:
A 58 year old Hazara woman is referred to you by her general practitioner with a note asking you to start an antipsychotic. She was resettled in Australia 14 months ago and her husband died of cancer four months ago.

Through an accredited interpreter she tells you that most nights she sees her husband sitting at the end of the bed and hears him speaking to her, usually telling her to look after the grandchildren. She finds these visits comforting and says several women in her community have described the same thing after a death. She sleeps about five hours, has lost 2 kg, and still cooks, prays and minds her grandchildren daily. She knows her husband has died and does not believe anyone is watching or following her.

data_table.Examination: Alert, tearful when speaking of her husband, speech normal in rate and form, no thought disorder, no responding to unseen stimuli during interview
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits, no cognitive concerns on collateral history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg at night and review the perceptual experiences in four weeks
options.rationale: An antipsychotic exposes her to metabolic and extrapyramidal harm for experiences that are neither distressing nor impairing and that carry no delusional elaboration. It would be indicated if the experiences were frightening, persecutory, or driving dysfunction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange urgent psychiatric admission for assessment of a suspected first episode of psychosis
options.rationale: She has preserved insight, intact daily function and no risk to herself or others, so an admission offers nothing that outpatient review does not. Admission would be driven by the label rather than by need. (Source: RANZCP position statement on the mental health of asylum seekers and refugees)
source_refs: RANZCP position statement on the mental health of asylum seekers and refugees

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for a depressive episode and review her symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Her sadness, sleep change and modest weight loss are proportionate to a recent death four months ago and she retains function and pleasure in caring for her grandchildren. An antidepressant becomes appropriate if a full depressive syndrome emerges or function declines. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Provide bereavement support with an accredited interpreter and review her again in two weeks
options.rationale: Seeing or hearing a deceased spouse is a recognised bereavement phenomenon, and here it is comforting, non delusional, culturally shared and occurring alongside preserved function, so support with planned review is the proportionate response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP position statement on the mental health of asylum seekers and refugees)
source_refs: RANZCP position statement on the mental health of asylum seekers and refugees

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the brain and formal cognitive testing before any management
options.rationale: Organic investigation is driven by cognitive decline, focal signs or an abrupt change in an older person, and her collateral history and screening bloods give no such indication. It would be the first step if the experiences were visual only with fluctuating cognition. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Perceptual experiences of a deceased person occur in a large minority of bereaved people and are more likely to be reported where a community regards continued contact with the dead as expected. They are distinguished from psychosis by preserved insight, the absence of delusional elaboration, congruent and comforting content, and intact function. Misreading them as psychosis is a well described source of over-diagnosis and over-treatment in people from refugee backgrounds, who may also be carrying multiple unprocessed losses from before and during flight. In context, the assessment task is not to decide whether an experience is unusual but whether it is impairing, and that question is answered with a cultural formulation rather than a symptom checklist.
key_points: Bereavement related perceptual experiences are common, insight preserving and congruent in content.
Psychosis is suggested by delusional elaboration, persecutory content, functional decline or loss of insight.
Cultural norms about contact with the dead change the meaning of the report but not the thresholds for treatment.
Multiple unacknowledged losses are the rule rather than the exception in people from refugee backgrounds.
explanation.pearls: A comforting, insight retaining experience of a deceased spouse does not meet criteria for prolonged grief disorder, which requires persistent intense yearning and functional impairment beyond twelve months in adults.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
RANZCP position statement on the mental health of asylum seekers and refugees

subtopic_detail: Low mood and fatigue at the post-arrival health assessment of a newly arrived refugee
stem:
A 31 year old woman from Myanmar attends your general practice five months after arriving on a humanitarian visa. Through an accredited interpreter she describes four months of tiredness, poor concentration, low mood and, in her words, thinking too much at night.

She spent six years in a camp in Thailand before resettlement. She denies suicidal thoughts and is caring for her two children, though she says everything takes more effort than it used to. Her Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score is 14. The post-arrival screening bloods requested at her first visit are back today.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, conjunctival pallor, no goitre, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 71 fL (80-100), ferritin 5 micrograms/L (30-300), vitamin D 29 nmol/L (more than 50), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, eosinophil count within normal limits, hepatitis B and strongyloides serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and arrange psychological review for her in six weeks
options.rationale: Starting an antidepressant before correcting a severe and symptomatic iron deficiency attributes reversible fatigue and poor concentration to mood alone. It becomes appropriate if symptoms persist once the deficiency is corrected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence iron replacement, investigate the cause, and reassess her mood in six weeks
options.rationale: A ferritin of 5 micrograms/L with microcytic anaemia is a sufficient and reversible explanation for fatigue and poor concentration, and the cause still needs identifying, so mood is formally reassessed once it is treated. (Source: Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases: Recommendations for Comprehensive Post-Arrival Health Assessment for People from Refugee-Like Backgrounds)
source_refs: Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases: Recommendations for Comprehensive Post-Arrival Health Assessment for People from Refugee-Like Backgrounds

options.text: Refer her to the state torture and trauma service and review her mood in six weeks
options.rationale: Specialist referral is valuable where there are trauma related symptoms, and she has described none on direct questioning with an interpreter. Referring on background rather than on symptoms displaces the treatable finding in front of you. (Source: Forum of Australian Services for Survivors of Torture and Trauma)
source_refs: Forum of Australian Services for Survivors of Torture and Trauma

options.text: Commence mirtazapine 15 mg at night for sleep and appetite and review her in six weeks
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is a second line antidepressant choice and here would sedate a woman whose fatigue has an unaddressed haematological cause. Its sleep and appetite profile is useful only once a primary mood disorder is established. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Repeat the questionnaire in six weeks and take no further action at this consultation
options.rationale: Watchful waiting leaves a severe iron deficiency untreated and its cause uninvestigated for another six weeks. Repeat scoring is a reasonable adjunct once the reversible contributor is being managed. (Source: RACGP Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice

explanation.summary: The Australian post-arrival health assessment for people of refugee background screens for iron deficiency, vitamin D deficiency, blood-borne viruses, latent tuberculosis, intestinal parasites including strongyloides and schistosoma, and incomplete immunisation, alongside mental health. Iron deficiency is common after prolonged camp residence and produces fatigue, poor concentration and irritability that overlap almost completely with depression. Somatic idioms such as thinking too much are widely used across Southeast Asian and African language groups and may describe distress, rumination, or a physical illness, which is why they are explored rather than translated straight into a diagnosis. In context, the risk in refugee health runs in both directions: attributing treatable physical illness to trauma, and attributing trauma related distress to physical illness.
key_points: Iron deficiency, vitamin D deficiency and parasitic infection are common after prolonged displacement and mimic depression.
The Patient Health Questionnaire 9 is not validated in every language group and does not by itself establish a diagnosis.
Somatic idioms of distress are explored with the person rather than mapped directly onto a diagnostic category.
Iron deficiency always requires a cause to be sought, not just replacement.
explanation.pearls: Strongyloides serology is checked before any course of systemic corticosteroid in a person of refugee background, because immunosuppression can convert chronic infection into fatal hyperinfection syndrome.

subtopic_detail: Episodic unresponsiveness in a survivor of torture already treated for trauma symptoms
stem:
A 44 year old Tamil man has been attending your clinic for two years with nightmares, hypervigilance and avoidance following detention and repeated beatings in his country of origin, which included blows to the head with a rifle butt. He takes sertraline 100 mg daily and has completed trauma focused therapy with an interpreter.

His wife reports that twice in the past month he has stopped responding mid conversation, stiffened, and had jerking of both arms for about a minute. Afterwards he was confused for twenty minutes and on one occasion he had bitten the side of his tongue. He has no memory of either episode. He has been getting daily headaches and losing his thread in conversation.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, cranial nerves intact, no focal limb weakness, gait normal, healed scar over the left parietal scalp
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, glucose and electrocardiogram within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose and re-refer him for trauma focused therapy with an interpreter
options.rationale: Escalating treatment for trauma symptoms does not account for tongue biting, post-event confusion and complete amnesia, which are not features of hyperarousal or avoidance. It would be reasonable if the episodes were reliving experiences with retained awareness. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Complex PTSD, Phoenix Australia)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Complex PTSD, Phoenix Australia

options.text: Attribute the episodes to dissociation and refer for grounding focused therapy with an interpreter
options.rationale: Dissociative episodes do not typically produce lateral tongue biting, sustained limb stiffening or a twenty minute confusional period. The distinction matters because a structural lesion would go undetected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence quetiapine 25 mg at night for the symptoms and review him in four weeks
options.rationale: Sedation at night addresses none of the daytime episodes and may obscure further events by blunting recall. Quetiapine also lowers the seizure threshold, which is the wrong direction here. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Reassure him that memory difficulty is expected and repeat a symptom checklist in three months
options.rationale: Reassurance without assessment leaves a potentially progressive intracranial cause unexamined for three months. Memory complaints alone might be watched, but not alongside witnessed convulsive episodes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for neurological assessment with brain imaging and an electroencephalogram this week
options.rationale: Witnessed stiffening with limb jerking, lateral tongue biting, post-event confusion and amnesia describe convulsive events requiring imaging and electroencephalography, particularly with a history of head injury and new daily headaches. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Survivors of torture carry a high burden of physical injury alongside psychological sequelae, including traumatic brain injury from blows to the head, suffocation and near drowning, and untreated fractures. Once a trauma diagnosis is recorded, new physical symptoms are readily folded into it, which delays the detection of epilepsy, chronic subdural collections, hearing loss and vestibular injury. A first presentation of convulsive episodes in an adult requires neuroimaging and electroencephalography regardless of psychiatric history. In context, a thorough physical history of what was done to a person is part of the mental health assessment, not separate from it.
key_points: Lateral tongue biting, sustained stiffening and prolonged post-event confusion point away from a dissociative explanation.
Head injury from torture is common and its consequences present years later.
A first adult convulsive episode requires neuroimaging and electroencephalography irrespective of a psychiatric diagnosis.
Attributing new physical symptoms to an existing trauma diagnosis is a recognised source of delayed diagnosis in this group.
explanation.pearls: Ask survivors of torture specifically about blows to the head, suffocation and near drowning, because each has a delayed neurological or respiratory sequela that a general systems review will miss.

Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Complex PTSD, Phoenix Australia
Australian Medicines Handbook

subtopic_detail: Adding pharmacotherapy after an adequate course of trauma focused psychological therapy
stem:
A 38 year old man who arrived from Iraq six years ago has been treated at your service for post-traumatic stress disorder. He has completed 14 sessions of trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy delivered with the same accredited interpreter throughout.

His avoidance has improved and he has returned to part time work. He still wakes most nights after nightmares, sleeps about four hours, and is easily startled. His Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Checklist score has fallen from 55 to 44 over four months and has been unchanged for the last six weeks. He is not drinking alcohol, has stable housing and permanent residency, and takes no regular medicines.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, no psychomotor slowing, no suicidal ideation elicited
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence diazepam 5 mg at night for sleep and review his symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not treat post-traumatic stress disorder, are associated with worse outcomes in this population, and add dependence risk to a chronic condition. Their only role is brief and situational. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Complex PTSD, Phoenix Australia)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Complex PTSD, Phoenix Australia

options.text: Commence quetiapine 25 mg at night for sleep and review his symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Low dose quetiapine is used widely as a hypnotic but carries metabolic risk without established benefit for core symptoms. Antipsychotics are considered only as adjuncts after adequate trials of first line agents. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg each morning and continue the psychological work in parallel
options.rationale: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is the recommended pharmacological addition when an adequate course of trauma focused therapy has produced partial response with residual hyperarousal, and it is added to rather than substituted for the therapy. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Complex PTSD, Phoenix Australia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Complex PTSD, Phoenix Australia

options.text: Commence prazosin 1 mg at night for nightmares and review his symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Prazosin has been trialled for trauma related nightmares but the evidence is inconsistent and it is not a first line pharmacological choice in Australian guidance. It is a later option for nightmares that persist despite an adequate antidepressant trial. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Complex PTSD, Phoenix Australia)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Complex PTSD, Phoenix Australia

options.text: Repeat an identical course of the same psychological therapy and review his symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: He has already had an adequate course and his score has plateaued for six weeks, so repeating it unchanged is unlikely to add benefit. Changing modality or adding pharmacotherapy is the usual response to a plateau. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Trauma focused psychological therapy is first line for post-traumatic stress disorder in Australia, including for people from refugee backgrounds, and is effective when delivered through a consistent accredited interpreter. Pharmacotherapy is recommended where psychological therapy is unavailable, declined, or has produced only partial response, and the first line agents are selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or venlafaxine. Where the person is still exposed to ongoing threat such as an unresolved visa process or family separation, stabilisation and practical advocacy take priority over both. In context, a plateau after an adequate course of therapy is an indication to add something, not to repeat the same course and hope for a different result.
key_points: Trauma focused psychological therapy is first line and pharmacotherapy is added for partial response.
Sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine and venlafaxine are the Australian first line pharmacological options.
Benzodiazepines are associated with worse outcomes and do not treat core symptoms.
Interpreter continuity across sessions is a determinant of whether trauma focused therapy works.
explanation.pearls: Allow eight to twelve weeks at an adequate dose before declaring a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor to have failed in post-traumatic stress disorder, which is longer than the four to six weeks used in depression.

sources.label: Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Acute Stress Disorder, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Complex PTSD, Phoenix Australia
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
Australian Medicines Handbook

subtopic_detail: Involuntary detention decision for an asylum seeker presenting with self harm
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in a New South Wales hospital. A 27 year old man who arrived by boat and is living in the community on a bridging visa is brought in by a friend at 9 pm after cutting his left forearm with a razor blade.

Through a telephone interpreter he says he has kept a box of his housemate's medication for weeks and intends to take it all tonight, and that nothing will change while his protection claim is unresolved. He is not intoxicated, has no psychotic symptoms, and is oriented and coherent. He says he wants to leave now and is standing by the door with his jacket on. His friend says he has not eaten for two days.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Three superficial forearm lacerations with haemostasis achieved, tearful, guarded, no thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas, electrolytes, paracetamol level and ethanol level within normal limits or not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Complete a mental health certificate under the Act and arrange transfer to a declared facility
options.rationale: He has a stated plan, access to means and an immediate intention to act, and is refusing to remain, which meets the threshold for detention on a medical practitioner's certificate for further assessment. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

options.text: Discharge him with a written safety plan and a community mental health appointment in three days
options.rationale: A safety plan cannot manage a disclosed plan with means already stockpiled and an intention to act tonight. It is the right approach once acute intent has resolved and means have been removed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Ask security to hold him while you seek advice from the immigration department about his visa
options.rationale: Visa status has no bearing on the operation of mental health legislation, and detention without a completed certificate has no lawful basis. Contacting immigration would also breach his confidentiality. (Source: RANZCP position statement on the mental health of asylum seekers and refugees)
source_refs: RANZCP position statement on the mental health of asylum seekers and refugees

options.text: Defer the decision until an on-site interpreter in his language can attend early tomorrow morning
options.rationale: A telephone interpreter has already allowed a clear risk assessment, and deferring overnight leaves him free to act on a stated plan. An on-site interpreter improves the next conversation but does not gate this decision. (Source: NSW Health Policy Directive: Interpreters - Standard Procedures for Working with Health Care Interpreters)
source_refs: NSW Health Policy Directive: Interpreters - Standard Procedures for Working with Health Care Interpreters

options.text: Contact the police to take him into custody under the Act as he refuses to remain
options.rationale: Police powers under the Act are for people in the community, whereas he is already in a hospital where a medical practitioner can complete the certificate. Police involvement would add a criminal justice dimension that is retraumatising for people who have fled state violence. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

explanation.summary: Under the New South Wales Mental Health Act 2007 a medical practitioner who has personally examined a person may complete a mental health certificate authorising detention in a declared mental health facility where the person appears to be mentally ill or mentally disordered and needs care, treatment or control for their own protection or that of others. The test is the risk and the need for care, not the diagnosis, and it is unaffected by visa status, Medicare eligibility or citizenship. Asylum seekers on bridging visas face compounding drivers of suicidality, including visa uncertainty, work restriction, family separation and destitution, and these are addressed alongside rather than instead of acute safety. In context, the decision to detain is made on the same legal test applied to anyone else, with an interpreter present so that the assessment on which it rests is sound.
key_points: A medical practitioner who has personally examined the person may complete the certificate authorising detention.
Visa status and Medicare eligibility have no bearing on the operation of mental health legislation.
A telephone interpreter is sufficient for an acute risk assessment when no on-site interpreter is available.
Stockpiled means plus stated intent to act tonight is a qualitatively different risk from historical self harm.
explanation.pearls: The certificate under the New South Wales Act is valid only if the practitioner has personally examined the person within the preceding 24 hours, which is why an assessment made solely on a colleague's handover will not support detention.

RANZCP position statement on the mental health of asylum seekers and refugees

subtopic_detail: Structuring the consultation when a parent answers for an adolescent from a resettled family
stem:
A 14 year old girl is brought to your general practice by her father because she has not attended school for six weeks. Her family arrived from Syria two years ago and she completed a year of intensive English before entering mainstream classes.

Her father answers every question you ask her, tells you she is simply lazy, and declines an interpreter for himself, saying his English is adequate. He reports that she complains of stomach aches and headaches on school mornings. When you ask her directly how she has been, she looks at her father and says nothing. Her physical examination is normal and she has grown along the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, abdomen soft and non tender, no organomegaly, no skin lesions
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, coeliac serology and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in this consultation?

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg daily for presumed anxiety and review her in four weeks
options.rationale: No history has yet been obtained from the young person herself, so there is no assessed diagnosis to treat. Pharmacotherapy follows assessment rather than substituting for it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer her to the school counsellor and review the attendance pattern again in four weeks
options.rationale: Referring her back into the setting she is avoiding, without knowing why, risks missing bullying, racism, a learning difficulty or an undisclosed home problem. School based support is a component of the plan once the reason is understood. (Source: headspace clinical guidance for young people)
source_refs: headspace clinical guidance for young people

options.text: Agree a graded return to school plan with her father and review the attendance in four weeks
options.rationale: A plan negotiated over her head is unlikely to be followed and repeats the dynamic that has stalled the consultation. Graded return works once the young person has contributed to the plan. (Source: headspace clinical guidance for young people)
source_refs: headspace clinical guidance for young people

options.text: Interview her alone for part of the consultation and offer her father an interpreter
options.rationale: Confidential time alone is standard practice in adolescent assessment and is the only way to obtain a history she can give freely, while a professional interpreter allows her father's account to be taken accurately rather than through her. (Source: RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice; headspace clinical guidance for young people)
source_refs: RACGP Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice
headspace clinical guidance for young people

options.text: Refer her to paediatrics for investigation of the headaches and abdominal pain in four weeks
options.rationale: Her examination and screening investigations are normal and the symptoms are school morning specific, so further organic investigation is low yield. It would be indicated if the pain were nocturnal, progressive or associated with growth failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Adolescent assessment includes time alone with the young person, with confidentiality and its limits explained in advance, and this holds regardless of family background. In families who have resettled, a young person is often the most fluent English speaker and can end up interpreting for the household, which places them in the position of relaying their own symptoms and any family conflict. Using a professional interpreter for the parent restores both the accuracy of the parent's account and the young person's right to a private consultation. School refusal in this group can reflect racism or bullying, an unrecognised learning difficulty, caring responsibilities at home, or trauma related symptoms in the young person or a parent. In context, structure the consultation first, because everything that follows depends on whose account you have actually heard.
key_points: Time alone with the adolescent is routine practice and is the point at which most disclosures happen.
Children should never be the interpreter for their own family's health consultations.
A parent declining an interpreter is common and is addressed by offering it as standard practice rather than as a judgement of their English.
School refusal requires the reason before the plan.
explanation.pearls: Free accredited interpreting is available to Australian general practices through the Translating and Interpreting Service National Doctors Priority Line, which removes the cost argument for using a family member.
