subtopic_detail: Interpreter selection when the allocated interpreter is known within the patient's community
stem:
A 29 year old Rohingya woman attends a refugee health clinic for her first mental health appointment. The nurse who booked the appointment recorded that she wanted to talk about what happened to her in the camp.

The accredited interpreter who arrives is a man from the same small community who greets her by her family name and mentions knowing her uncle. She lowers her gaze, answers in single words, and says everything is fine. Earlier, in the waiting room, she had told the nurse through a phone interpreter that she had not been sleeping and had been having bad memories. Her brother is waiting outside and has offered to help if needed.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, guarded, reduced eye contact, no psychomotor agitation
data_table.Investigations: Post-arrival screening bloods within normal limits, pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue with the booked interpreter and revisit the sensitive history at a later appointment
options.rationale: Deferring the disclosure keeps the same barrier in place and risks her not returning, since a first appointment that goes nowhere is a common point of disengagement. Continuing would be reasonable only for a routine physical review. (Source: NSW Health Policy Directive: Interpreters - Standard Procedures for Working with Health Care Interpreters)
source_refs: NSW Health Policy Directive: Interpreters - Standard Procedures for Working with Health Care Interpreters

options.text: Change to a female accredited interpreter by telephone today and continue the assessment
options.rationale: A telephone interpreter from outside her community removes both the gender and the confidentiality barrier immediately, and can be arranged during the appointment rather than at the cost of another visit. (Source: NSW Health Policy Directive: Interpreters - Standard Procedures for Working with Health Care Interpreters; Forum of Australian Services for Survivors of Torture and Trauma)
source_refs: NSW Health Policy Directive: Interpreters - Standard Procedures for Working with Health Care Interpreters
Forum of Australian Services for Survivors of Torture and Trauma

options.text: Ask her adult brother in the waiting room to interpret for the remainder of the consultation
options.rationale: A family member is not an accredited interpreter, cannot be held to a confidentiality standard, and is the least safe option where sexual violence may be disclosed. Family interpreting also alters what the person is willing to say. (Source: NSW Health Policy Directive: Interpreters - Standard Procedures for Working with Health Care Interpreters)
source_refs: NSW Health Policy Directive: Interpreters - Standard Procedures for Working with Health Care Interpreters

options.text: Proceed in English without an interpreter, using short sentences and written information sheets
options.rationale: Conversational capacity in a second language does not extend to describing trauma or understanding treatment options, and written material assumes a literacy level that cannot be presumed. Unassisted English would guarantee an incomplete history. (Source: NSW Health Policy Directive: Interpreters - Standard Procedures for Working with Health Care Interpreters)
source_refs: NSW Health Policy Directive: Interpreters - Standard Procedures for Working with Health Care Interpreters

options.text: Reschedule her to a clinic in three months when a local female interpreter becomes available
options.rationale: A three month delay for a woman who has already signalled why she came is the main mechanism by which this group falls out of care. Telephone interpreting makes the wait unnecessary. (Source: Forum of Australian Services for Survivors of Torture and Trauma)
source_refs: Forum of Australian Services for Survivors of Torture and Trauma

explanation.summary: Accredited interpreting is the standard for any consultation where language is a barrier, and the interpreter's gender, dialect, ethnicity, religion and political affiliation can all matter in small communities where people know each other. Telephone and video interpreting solve most of these problems because the interpreter can be located in another state. Survivors of sexual violence and of politically motivated persecution are particularly likely to withhold information from an interpreter who moves in the same social circles. In context, confirm at the start of the consultation that the person is comfortable with the interpreter provided, because the moment they are not, everything recorded afterwards is unreliable.
key_points: Check acceptability of the interpreter with the person at the start, not after the consultation has stalled.
Telephone or video interpreting from interstate resolves community overlap and gender preference on the day.
Family members, and especially children, are never used as interpreters for a mental health assessment.
Conversational English is not the same as the capacity to describe trauma or weigh treatment options.
explanation.pearls: A person who spoke freely with a phone interpreter in the waiting room and then goes quiet when an in-person interpreter arrives has given you the answer about which arrangement to use.

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a non-trough lithium level during fasting and concurrent anti-inflammatory use
stem:
A 34 year old man who was resettled from Afghanistan seven years ago has bipolar I disorder that has been stable on lithium carbonate 750 mg at night for three years, with levels consistently between 0.6 and 0.8 mmol/L.

For the past ten days he has been fasting between dawn and sunset for Ramadan and has moved his lithium to 4.30 am so that he can take it with the pre-dawn meal. He has continued landscaping work outdoors through a heatwave. He bought ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily five days ago for back pain.

He presents at 9.30 am with two days of nausea, a coarse tremor of both hands and unsteadiness on his feet. His speech is clear, he is fully oriented, and there is no myoclonus or rigidity.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, normal tone, reflexes normal and symmetrical, no clonus, alert and oriented
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 1.3 mmol/L taken at 9.30 am (therapeutic trough 0.6-0.8), sodium 147 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 116 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate 64 mL/min/1.73m2, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, electrocardiogram sinus tachycardia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management today?

options.text: Continue the current dose, since the sample was taken five hours after his dose rather than at trough
options.rationale: A non-trough sample overstates the trough concentration, but he has clinical features of toxicity with a rising sodium and creatinine, so the number is not the reason to act and discounting it ignores the examination. Timing would be the deciding issue only in an asymptomatic person with normal renal function. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Halve the lithium dose, continue the ibuprofen for his back pain, and repeat the level in two weeks
options.rationale: Leaving the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug in place preserves the interaction that reduced lithium clearance in the first place, and a two week interval is far too long for someone symptomatic today. Dose halving without removing the precipitant treats the symptom of the problem. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer him for urgent haemodialysis on the basis of the level and his reduced renal function
options.rationale: Haemodialysis is reserved for levels above about 2.5 mmol/L with significant symptoms, or for severe neurological features, renal failure or an inability to excrete. His level and mild cerebellar signs fall well short of that threshold. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Switch him from lithium to sodium valproate today and arrange psychiatric review within two weeks
options.rationale: Abandoning a mood stabiliser that has held him well for three years, because of a reversible drug and dehydration interaction, risks relapse and solves nothing acutely. A switch is considered for persistent renal impairment or repeated toxicity, not for a single explained episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Withhold lithium, cease the ibuprofen, rehydrate him, and repeat a 12 hour trough level tomorrow
options.rationale: Both reversible drivers of reduced lithium clearance are removed, volume is restored, and a correctly timed trough taken 12 hours after a dose gives the number on which redosing can safely be based. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Lithium is reabsorbed with sodium in the proximal tubule, so anything that reduces effective circulating volume or sodium delivery raises the concentration: dehydration, a low salt intake, vomiting, diarrhoea, and the classic interacting drugs, which are non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, thiazide diuretics and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors. Fasting between dawn and sunset in hot weather while working outdoors combines several of these at once, and the dose timing shift that fasting requires also invalidates the standard 12 hour trough sample. Most people who fast for Ramadan wish to continue, and Islamic teaching exempts those who are unwell, so the clinical task is to plan the dosing and hydration in advance rather than to argue about the fast. In context, the level is interpreted alongside the sampling time, the renal function and the examination, and the examination wins when they disagree.
key_points: A lithium level taken other than 12 hours after the dose overstates the trough and cannot be used for dose adjustment.
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, thiazides and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors reduce lithium clearance and are the usual precipitants.
Rising sodium and creatinine alongside tremor and ataxia indicate volume depletion with reduced clearance rather than a laboratory artefact.
Haemodialysis is reserved for levels above about 2.5 mmol/L with significant symptoms or for severe neurological or renal compromise.
explanation.pearls: Plan lithium dosing before Ramadan begins rather than during it: moving the whole dose to the pre-dawn or post-sunset meal, with a documented sampling time, keeps levels interpretable for the month.

subtopic_detail: Concurrent diagnosis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in an adult with autism
stem:
A 24 year old woman was diagnosed with autism last year after presenting with exhaustion following social contact. She now describes lifelong difficulty sustaining attention, losing essential items and leaving tasks unfinished, which her primary school reports and her mother both confirm.

These difficulties affect her university course and her casual job equally. A clinician she saw previously told her that attention problems are simply part of autism and cannot be diagnosed separately. She is not depressed, sleeps well, and takes no medicines.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, mental state examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, electrolytes and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Explain that attention symptoms within autism cannot be separately diagnosed or treated
options.rationale: This restriction was removed when DSM-5 replaced DSM-IV, and repeating it denies her access to effective treatment. It described the diagnostic rules that applied before 2013. (Source: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.text: Repeat the autism assessment to check whether the original diagnosis was correct
options.rationale: Nothing in her history casts doubt on the autism diagnosis, and repeating it does not address the attention symptoms. Re-assessment is warranted when the original findings conflict with the developmental history. (Source: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.text: Arrange an assessment for a co-occurring attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
options.rationale: DSM-5 permits both diagnoses concurrently, and around a third of autistic people meet criteria for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, which is treatable in its own right. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, AADPA)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, AADPA

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and review her concentration in six weeks
options.rationale: She has no depressive or anxiety disorder, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors do not improve inattention. This would treat a diagnosis she does not have. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for cognitive testing to see whether an intellectual disability explains this
options.rationale: She is completing a university course and holds a job, which is inconsistent with unrecognised intellectual disability. Cognitive testing is indicated where the developmental history and current function suggest a global deficit. (Source: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

explanation.summary: DSM-IV prohibited diagnosing attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in a person with autism, and DSM-5 removed that exclusion in 2013 because the two conditions co-occur in roughly a third of cases. The legacy rule persists in clinical folklore and is a common reason that autistic adults, particularly women diagnosed late, never have their attention symptoms assessed. Treating co-occurring attention deficit hyperactivity disorder improves function in autistic people, although adverse effects of stimulants, including appetite suppression and irritability, are somewhat more frequent. In context, a late autism diagnosis often explains part of a person's history but rarely all of it, and the remainder deserves the same assessment anyone else would get.
key_points: DSM-5 permits concurrent diagnosis of autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder; DSM-IV did not.
Around a third of autistic people also meet criteria for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
Childhood evidence of symptoms is still required, and collateral or school records supply it.
Attributing every symptom to an established neurodevelopmental diagnosis is the diagnostic overshadowing error.
explanation.pearls: Stimulant response rates are lower and adverse effect rates higher in autistic people with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, so start at the lowest dose and titrate in smaller increments than usual.

subtopic_detail: Starting dose of an antidepressant for anxiety in an autistic adult
stem:
A 29 year old autistic man has generalised anxiety that has persisted despite 12 sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for autistic adults. He worries most days about work and travel, sleeps poorly and has stopped catching trains.

He lives independently and works as a data analyst. At 22 he was prescribed fluoxetine 20 mg daily and stopped it after five days because he felt wound up and could not keep still, which resolved within two days of stopping. He drinks no alcohol and takes no other medicines. He would like to try medication again alongside continuing therapy.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows anxious mood, no psychomotor agitation, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits, electrocardiogram within normal limits

lead_in: Which prescribing plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Sertraline 25 mg daily, increasing slowly after four weeks if it is tolerated
options.rationale: Autistic adults show higher rates of activation and other adverse effects on serotonergic agents, and his previous early reaction supports starting at half the usual dose with a slower titration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg daily, increasing to 100 mg after two weeks if it is tolerated
options.rationale: A standard starting dose with rapid escalation is the regimen most likely to reproduce the activation that ended his previous trial and lose him to treatment altogether. This schedule suits a person with no history of early intolerance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg as required for anxiety, with review of his response after four weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not treat generalised anxiety disorder in the medium term and carry dependence risk, and paradoxical disinhibition is more common in neurodevelopmental conditions. Short term use is limited to crisis situations. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Risperidone 0.5 mg at night, increasing to 1 mg after two weeks if it is tolerated
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not a treatment for generalised anxiety disorder and expose him to metabolic and extrapyramidal harm. Their limited autism indication is for severe irritability and aggression, which he does not have. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Propranolol 10 mg three times daily, with review of his response after four weeks
options.rationale: Beta blockade attenuates autonomic symptoms but does not treat the cognitive component of generalised anxiety disorder. It is useful mainly for discrete performance situations. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Anxiety disorders affect around 40 percent of autistic adults and are a common reason for a first psychiatric presentation, often years before the autism itself is recognised. Psychological therapy adapted for autistic people, with more concrete language, visual supports and longer sessions, is first line, and a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is added when response is incomplete. Autistic people report higher rates of adverse effects, particularly activation, gastrointestinal upset and sensory intensification, so starting at half the usual dose and titrating slowly improves the chance that a trial reaches an effective dose. In context, a medication abandoned in the first week because of activation is usually a titration failure rather than a drug failure, and it is worth revisiting.
key_points: Start serotonergic agents at half the usual dose in autistic adults and titrate more slowly.
Early activation is a titration problem and does not exclude a later successful trial of the same class.
Antipsychotics in autism are reserved for severe irritability or aggression, not anxiety.
Adapted cognitive behavioural therapy remains first line and continues alongside medication.
explanation.pearls: Allow four weeks at the starting dose before the first increase in an autistic adult, as the activation window closes within two weeks in most people who push through it.

Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

subtopic_detail: Restlessness emerging after an antidepressant dose increase in an autistic adult
stem:
A 31 year old autistic woman was started on sertraline 50 mg daily twelve days ago for a moderate depressive episode. Three days ago a colleague increased the dose to 100 mg because her partner reported that she had become more agitated.

She now paces the house from morning until night, has slept four hours in three days, and repeatedly stands up and sits down during your consultation. She describes a feeling in her legs that only walking relieves, and says it is nothing like her usual hand movements, which she has done since childhood and finds calming. Her partner says the pacing started two days after the first prescription and has worsened since the increase. She has no thoughts of self harm and her mood is unchanged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No tremor, normal tone, reflexes normal and symmetrical, no clonus, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and creatine kinase within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose to 150 mg daily and review her symptoms again in one week
options.rationale: Escalating the causative drug is the classic error when drug induced restlessness is misread as worsening illness, and it predictably intensifies the symptom. Escalation would be right if this were a partial response with unchanged restlessness pre-dating the prescription. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add diazepam 5 mg twice daily and continue the sertraline at 100 mg daily for now
options.rationale: A benzodiazepine may blunt the distress but leaves the drug driving it in place at full dose. It is an adjunct once the offending dose has been reduced, not a substitute for doing so. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Add quetiapine 25 mg at night for sleep and continue the sertraline at 100 mg daily
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are themselves a leading cause of this syndrome, so adding one risks compounding rather than relieving it. Sedation would also obscure the response to any later dose reduction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reduce the sertraline dose immediately and review her in person within 48 hours
options.rationale: The restlessness began two days after the drug was started, worsened with the increase, is subjectively located in the legs and is relieved by movement, which identifies it as drug induced and makes dose reduction the definitive treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Add propranolol 10 mg three times daily and continue the sertraline at 100 mg daily
options.rationale: Propranolol has a genuine role in this syndrome but as an adjunct after the offending agent has been reduced or withdrawn, which is the distinction between symptomatic cover and definitive treatment. Using it alone leaves the cause running. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Akathisia is an inner restlessness relieved by movement that is most familiar as an antipsychotic adverse effect but occurs with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors too, typically within the first two weeks or after a dose increase. It is dangerous because it is readily misread as worsening anxiety or agitation, prompting a dose increase that makes it worse, and because it is associated with suicidal acts. In autistic people the risk of misreading is higher still, since repetitive self-soothing movements may be mistaken for it, and the discriminating features are the timing relative to the prescription, the subjective inner restlessness, and the fact that the movement is unwanted rather than calming. In context, whenever a symptom worsens after a psychotropic dose is increased, the drug is a suspect before the illness is.
key_points: Akathisia is subjective inner restlessness relieved by movement, not simply observed overactivity.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors cause it, usually within two weeks of starting or increasing.
Definitive treatment is reducing or ceasing the causative agent; propranolol and benzodiazepines are adjuncts.
Long standing self-soothing repetitive movements in an autistic person are distinguished by being wanted and unchanged in timing.
explanation.pearls: Akathisia carries an association with suicidal acts independent of the underlying depression, which is why it warrants review within 48 hours rather than at the next routine appointment.

Australian Medicines Handbook

subtopic_detail: New physical symptoms in an autistic adult already labelled as anxious
stem:
A 27 year old autistic man attends with four months of abdominal pain and 6 kg of unintentional weight loss. Two clinicians have told him the pain is anxiety and advised breathing exercises.

He finds it hard to localise the pain and describes it as a feeling that something is wrong low down in his belly. He has been opening his bowels four to six times a day, sometimes waking him at night, which is a change from his lifelong routine of once each morning. He has no history of an eating disorder and his appetite is unchanged. His mother says he stopped going to his weekly board game group two months ago because of the pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 19.4 kg/m2, mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no mass, no perianal abnormality seen
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (130-175), mean cell volume 76 fL (80-100), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (30-300), C-reactive protein 34 mg/L (less than 5), albumin 32 g/L (35-50), coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer him to a psychologist for anxiety focused therapy and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Nocturnal symptoms, weight loss, anaemia and a raised inflammatory marker are not produced by anxiety, so this repeats the attribution that has already delayed his diagnosis by four months. Therapy is appropriate for anxiety once organic disease has been excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg daily for anxiety and review his symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Prescribing for a presumed psychiatric cause while objective abnormalities remain unexplained compounds the delay and adds gastrointestinal adverse effects that will confuse the picture. It would be appropriate once a physical cause has been excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer him urgently for specialist assessment and endoscopic investigation of the bowel
options.rationale: Weight loss, nocturnal bowel symptoms, iron deficiency anaemia, a raised C-reactive protein and a low albumin together constitute alarm features requiring specialist assessment and direct visualisation of the bowel. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Commence oral iron and repeat the full blood count in eight weeks without investigation
options.rationale: Replacing iron without establishing why a young man is iron deficient treats the consequence and conceals the trend. Iron deficiency in a man of any age always requires the cause to be sought. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Explain that the symptoms reflect differences in bodily perception and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Differences in interoception are real in autistic people and explain vague localisation, but they do not explain anaemia, weight loss or an inflammatory response. Using them as the whole explanation is the overshadowing error in its most persuasive form. (Source: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

explanation.summary: Diagnostic overshadowing is the attribution of new symptoms to an existing neurodevelopmental or psychiatric diagnosis, and it is a documented contributor to the reduced life expectancy of autistic adults. Autistic people frequently describe interoceptive differences, so pain may be reported vaguely, late, or through a change in behaviour such as withdrawal from a valued activity, which is easily read as social anxiety. The safeguard is to anchor decisions to objective data rather than to the quality of the symptom description. In context, a change in a long established routine reported by a person or their family is a clinical sign in its own right and deserves the weight that a clearly described symptom would get.
key_points: Weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anaemia and raised inflammatory markers are never explained by anxiety.
Iron deficiency in an adult man always requires investigation of the source.
Interoceptive differences change how symptoms are described, not whether they have a physical cause.
Withdrawal from a valued routine activity may be the presenting sign of physical illness in an autistic adult.
explanation.pearls: Ask an autistic patient and their family what has changed in their routine rather than how bad the pain is, because loss of a fixed weekly activity is often the most reliable severity measure available.

subtopic_detail: Functional decline after a role change in an autistic adult on a stable antidepressant
stem:
A 34 year old autistic woman has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for two years for a depressive episode, with full remission until three months ago. Four months ago she was promoted from a solo laboratory role into a client facing position in an open plan office.

She now sleeps twelve hours on weekends, has stopped cooking and has let her driving lapse because it takes too much effort. At work she has started making errors. On a two week holiday last month she felt like herself again within four days and resumed cooking. She still enjoys her home routines and her weight is stable. She has no suicidal thoughts and denies guilt or worthlessness.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows reactive mood, normal speech rate, no psychomotor retardation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose to 150 mg daily and review her mood again in four weeks
options.rationale: Her mood is reactive, she recovered fully on leave and she has no core depressive features, so this is not an inadequately treated depressive episode. Dose escalation is the right move when symptoms persist independently of the environment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange workplace adjustments with a graded reduction in demands and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Skills that were previously automatic have been lost in proportion to a sustained rise in sensory and social demand and recovered within days of that demand being removed, so reducing the load is the intervention that matches the pattern. (Source: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.text: Add quetiapine 25 mg at night and review her mood and function in four weeks
options.rationale: She is sleeping excessively rather than too little, so a sedative addresses the opposite problem and adds metabolic risk. Augmentation is considered only for genuine treatment resistant depression. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer her for a repeat diagnostic assessment and review her mood and function in four weeks
options.rationale: Her autism diagnosis is established and re-assessment would not change the management of a demand related decline. It is indicated only where the original diagnosis conflicts with the developmental history. (Source: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.text: Commence lithium augmentation at 500 mg at night and review her mood again in four weeks
options.rationale: Augmentation with lithium follows two adequate antidepressant trials in a persisting depressive episode, none of which describes her situation. It would also commit her to monitoring she does not need. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Autistic adults describe periods of profound exhaustion with loss of previously reliable skills after sustained periods of high social and sensory demand, often following a promotion, a move, or the end of a long masking effort. The pattern is distinguished from a depressive episode by the environmental contingency, the preserved capacity for pleasure in low demand settings, the rapid recovery when demands are removed, and the loss of practical skills out of proportion to mood. Treating it as treatment resistant depression leads to escalating pharmacotherapy that does not work and delays the adjustments that do. In context, promotion out of a role a person was thriving in is a recognisable trigger, and the fix is usually structural rather than pharmacological.
key_points: Environmental contingency and rapid recovery on leave argue against an inadequately treated depressive episode.
Loss of automatic practical skills out of proportion to mood is characteristic of demand related exhaustion.
Workplace adjustments are available under the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 and can be requested with a supporting letter.
Escalating antidepressant doses for a demand driven decline delays effective management.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically what happened on the last holiday: recovery within days of removing demand, followed by decline within a week of returning, separates this pattern from a depressive episode more reliably than any rating scale.

subtopic_detail: Gender assessment request from an autistic adult declined by the referral service
stem:
A 26 year old autistic person who uses they and them pronouns is referred back to you by a gender service, which has written that assessment should wait until the autism is better understood.

They have identified as non binary consistently since the age of 16, have used their current name for four years, and describe persistent distress about their chest and voice. They live independently, manage their own finances and work full time in logistics. They understand the effects of hormone therapy, its reversible and irreversible components, and its effect on fertility, and they can explain these back to you accurately. They have no psychotic symptoms and no current depressive episode.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, mental state examination shows congruent affect and no perceptual disturbance
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, lipids and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Defer the gender assessment until a further autism specific assessment has been completed
options.rationale: An established autism diagnosis does not create an unanswered question that must be resolved first, and deferral on this basis is the exact barrier that keeps autistic people out of gender services. Further assessment is warranted only if a specific capacity concern exists. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Explain that gender affirming hormone therapy is not offered to autistic people
options.rationale: No Australian standard excludes autistic people from gender affirming care, and autistic people are several times more likely than others to be gender diverse. The statement is factually wrong as well as discriminatory. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

options.text: Refer them for social skills training before revisiting the request for gender assessment
options.rationale: Nothing in the presentation indicates a social skills need, and the referral would delay the request without addressing it. It also implies that the gender identity is a product of social difficulty. (Source: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.text: Arrange a capacity assessment by an independent psychiatrist before taking any further steps
options.rationale: Capacity is presumed in an adult and is assessed decision by decision by the treating clinician, and this person has already demonstrated understanding and reasoning about the treatment. A formal assessment is indicated when a specific doubt arises, not by diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria)
source_refs: RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria

options.text: Proceed with gender assessment, adjusting the communication format and appointment length
options.rationale: A consistent identity over ten years, demonstrated understanding of the treatment and independent function support proceeding, with adjustments such as written information in advance and longer appointments to make the assessment accessible. (Source: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy)
source_refs: AusPATH Australian Informed Consent Standards of Care for Gender Affirming Hormone Therapy

explanation.summary: Autistic people are several times more likely than non-autistic people to be trans or gender diverse, and the overlap is large enough that gender services and autism services routinely see the same individuals. Being autistic is not a reason to delay or refuse gender assessment; it is a reason to adapt how the assessment is conducted, with written information provided in advance, longer or split appointments, concrete language, a support person if wanted, and attention to sensory aspects of any procedure. Capacity is decision specific and is demonstrated by understanding, retaining, weighing and communicating a choice, all of which this person has shown. In context, the harm of unnecessary gatekeeping is measurable, since autistic trans people report higher rates of unsupervised hormone use and of self harm than trans people who are not autistic.
key_points: Autistic people are over-represented among trans and gender diverse populations.
An autism diagnosis is a reason to adapt the assessment, not to defer it.
Capacity is presumed in adults, assessed decision by decision, and is not displaced by a diagnosis.
Unnecessary gatekeeping predicts unsupervised hormone use and disengagement from care.
explanation.pearls: Send written information before the appointment and allow the person to answer in writing: an autistic person who appears uncertain when questioned face to face often demonstrates full understanding when the format changes.

RANZCP position statement on the mental health needs of people experiencing gender dysphoria
Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

subtopic_detail: Attention symptoms first appearing in middle adult life
stem:
A 41 year old accountant asks to be referred for assessment after scoring highly on an online attention questionnaire. For three years he has been forgetful, easily distracted, irritable with his children and unable to finish reports, and he has twice fallen asleep at his desk in the afternoon.

He brought his school reports, which describe him as attentive and consistently near the top of his class, and his mother recalls no difficulties. His wife says he snores loudly and that she has watched him stop breathing several times a night. He drinks two standard drinks most evenings and his body mass index is 34 kg/m2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Neck circumference 44 cm, oropharynx crowded, no goitre, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function, iron studies and fasting glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a formal sleep study before proceeding with any attention deficit assessment
options.rationale: Witnessed apnoeas, loud snoring, daytime sleepiness, obesity and hypertension point to a sleep disorder that reproduces every one of his cognitive complaints and is treatable. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, AADPA)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, AADPA

options.text: Refer him to a psychiatrist for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder assessment
options.rationale: The diagnosis requires several symptoms before the age of twelve, and his school reports and his mother's account both exclude that. Referral would be appropriate if childhood evidence were absent rather than contradictory. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, AADPA)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, AADPA

options.text: Commence a trial of lisdexamfetamine 30 mg each morning and review in four weeks
options.rationale: A stimulant improves alertness in almost anyone, so a positive response would not confirm a diagnosis, and it would raise his already elevated blood pressure. Stimulants follow a confirmed diagnosis rather than serving as a diagnostic test. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for a presumed depressive episode and review shortly
options.rationale: He describes irritability and poor concentration without low mood, anhedonia or hopelessness, so the depressive criteria are not met. Treating presumptively would delay the investigation his history points towards. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure him that attention symptoms at this age are age related and review annually
options.rationale: Reassurance leaves untreated obstructive sleep apnoea with its cardiovascular and accident risks, and three years of functional decline is not an age effect at 41. Annual review suits a stable, explained and non-progressive complaint. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, AADPA)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, AADPA

explanation.summary: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition, so DSM-5 requires several symptoms to have been present before the age of twelve and to cause impairment in two or more settings. Adult onset attention complaints therefore prompt a search for what has changed, and the usual candidates are obstructive sleep apnoea, a mood or anxiety disorder, alcohol or other substance use, thyroid disease, iron deficiency, perimenopause and medication adverse effects. Online screening questionnaires are sensitive and unspecific, and they describe a symptom pattern rather than establishing its onset. In context, the recent surge in adult referrals means the diagnostic task is now as often about excluding treatable mimics as about recognising a genuinely missed lifelong condition.
key_points: Childhood onset before age twelve is required, and contradictory collateral evidence rules the diagnosis out rather than leaving it open.
Obstructive sleep apnoea reproduces inattention, irritability and poor task completion and is directly treatable.
A symptomatic response to a stimulant does not confirm the diagnosis, because stimulants improve alertness in anyone.
Online questionnaires describe current symptoms and cannot establish developmental onset.
explanation.pearls: Ask for school reports at the first appointment: they are the most accessible source of the childhood evidence the diagnosis requires and frequently settle the question before any specialist referral is made.

subtopic_detail: Self-injurious behaviour after a change of accommodation in a minimally speaking autistic adult
stem:
You are asked to review a 23 year old autistic man who moved into a new supported accommodation house five weeks ago. Over the past three weeks he has been striking the side of his head with his palm, leaving bruising.

He communicates with single words and a picture based system. Staff record that the striking happens almost entirely between four and six in the afternoon in the shared lounge, when the television is on and the staff shift changes. His previous house had a quiet room and a visual timetable on the wall, and neither is in place at the new house. A dental review and a physical examination last week were unremarkable. The house manager has asked you to prescribe something to be given when he becomes distressed.

data_table.Examination: Bruising over the left temporal scalp, no laceration, ears and oropharynx normal, abdomen soft, gait normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, liver function, thyroid function and urine microscopy within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence risperidone 0.5 mg at night and review the behaviour in four weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotic use to control behaviour without a psychiatric indication is chemical restraint and is a regulated restrictive practice. It is considered only after environmental and communication strategies have been tried and have failed. (Source: NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission: Regulated Restrictive Practices Guide)
source_refs: NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission: Regulated Restrictive Practices Guide

options.text: Commence diazepam 2 mg as required and review the behaviour in four weeks
options.rationale: A benzodiazepine given as required for behaviour is also chemical restraint, and paradoxical disinhibition is more common in this group. Its use is restricted to defined short term situations under an authorised plan. (Source: NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission: Regulated Restrictive Practices Guide)
source_refs: NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission: Regulated Restrictive Practices Guide

options.text: Arrange admission to an inpatient mental health unit for assessment and behavioural stabilisation
options.rationale: An unfamiliar, noisy ward removes the environmental predictability that is already the problem and typically escalates distress. Admission is reserved for a psychiatric illness or a risk that cannot be managed in the community. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Developmental disability)

options.text: Arrange a functional behaviour assessment with sensory and communication supports in place
options.rationale: The behaviour is confined to one predictable time, place and set of conditions and followed the loss of a quiet space and a visual timetable, which identifies environmental triggers and an unmet communication need as the targets. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Developmental disability; NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission: Regulated Restrictive Practices Guide)
source_refs: NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission: Regulated Restrictive Practices Guide

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and review the behaviour and sleep in four weeks
options.rationale: There is no evidence of a depressive or anxiety disorder, and serotonergic agents have not been shown to reduce repetitive or self-injurious behaviour in autism. Activation may make the behaviour worse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Self-injurious behaviour in a minimally speaking autistic adult is communication until proven otherwise, and the assessment sequence is to exclude pain, then to map the antecedents, behaviour and consequences before considering any medicine. Common physical causes include dental disease, otitis, constipation, gastro-oesophageal reflux, headache and menstrual pain, and these are looked for with an examination and targeted tests rather than a symptom report. Where the behaviour is tightly linked to time of day, setting and sensory conditions, environmental and communication changes are both the diagnostic test and the treatment. In context, prescribing a psychotropic to manage behaviour without a psychiatric indication is chemical restraint, which in Australia is a regulated restrictive practice requiring authorisation, a behaviour support plan and reporting.
key_points: Exclude physical pain first: dental disease, ear infection, constipation and reflux are the usual culprits.
A predictable time, place and sensory context points to an environmental trigger rather than an illness.
Psychotropics given to control behaviour without a psychiatric indication meet the definition of chemical restraint.
Risperidone has an evidence base for severe irritability and aggression in autism, but only after behavioural strategies have failed and with metabolic monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Ask what changed in the environment in the weeks before the behaviour started, because the removal of a visual timetable or a quiet space explains more escalations in supported accommodation than any new symptom does.
